text:
Sooner or later, the interviewer stops asking for code. They hand you a number and ask what it means, and then how you'd explain it to someone who has never written a query. There are fourteen questions to be ready for. Ten of them hide a trap, so we'll take those slowly. The other four get one answer each, in a rapid-fire round. The first is about the number every report leads with.

Question one. When would you report the median instead of the mean? When the data is skewed. Here are five hundred orders. Most are small, and a long tail runs out past a hundred dollars. The median order is twenty-three eleven. The mean is twenty-six fifty-eight, dragged to the right by the tail. Only a hundred and eighty-one of the five hundred orders are above it. Income, house prices and session lengths all look like this. Report the median as the typical value, and both when the gap between them is the story. Next, two numbers that move together.

Question two. Explain correlation does not imply causation, with an example. Two hundred days. On days when more ice cream sells, more people drown. The correlation is point five seven. Ice cream doesn't cause drowning. Hot weather drives both: more people buy ice cream, and more people swim. The hot days sit together, top right. Temperature is the confounder. Hold temperature fixed, and the link all but vanishes: point zero eight. To argue a cause, you need an experiment, like an A B test, or a careful causal design.
